item.content:encoded:
Y'know, I realized today I never commented on this, but someone mentioned it again and I suddenly wanted to: This is among my favorite SCP-001s on the site.

It's hard to pin down exactly why. It feels personal — intimate — in a way SCP-001s aren't meant to be, but still works. The final note from Mary Nakayama's computer felt both incredibly heart-breaking yet simultaneously deeply empowering. She might be the only person on earth who could sincerely say she literally became her own savior.

Anyway, I just wanted to say how much I love this particular SCP-001. Thank you for writing it!

item.content:encoded:
While I agree with the above user that the progression is steep, we do see a notable time gap in the saves that Mary spent debating her godhood. Furthermore, the final note clearly is meant to imply that she isn't becoming god for power-lust or for a selfish desire, but out of a desire to protect humanity. I think adding more changes would only serve to bloat the article.

To be frank I consider this to be, while not the more interesting 001, the best 001 Proposal for the following reasons; it clearly has an actual reason behind it being 001 other than 'The world has ended', or 'it really was the first', or 'and that's why the foundation works the way it does'. Additionally the unique anomaly alone makes for an interesting SCP that is further enhanced by its effects. To put it more clearly, it's a simple anomaly that is very deep in its scope.

+1

As much as I like the concept of this SCP, I feel like there isn't enough time between "I get a promotion! I get $5! I get a vacation!" and "I BECOME GOD". The progression is far too steep. Having a few more dramatic steps ("SCP [REDACTED] will cease to exist" alongside a note saying no SCP was ever cataloged or a safe SCP is in that spot, Mary making the person who left her die, "world hunger will be ended") would make the ending feel a touch more in place.

The last addendum also didn't feel like it fleshed anything out for me; its insertion was too sudden, the context surrounding it too minimal. If you're going to add in a backstory or a reason for Mary to ascend to godhood, I think there should be more to it. This just made me more confused. I do love the implication that this is a self-fulfilling prophecy of sorts, though.

I genuinely love the concept here and think what you've done with it is compelling, but ultimately I think it just escalated far too quickly and didn't really do enough to make Mary interesting. Novote.

They did. We called it the Cornwall Incident: a Type Black, in alliance with a large coven of Type Blue allies, attempted a massive magical working to end human pain and conflict. The end result threatened the end of the human spirit.

You see, war and hunger all derive from dissatisfaction with your current status quo. When you are completely satisfied with your status quo, you have no motivation or desire to do… anything. Getting rid of war and hunger and pain required getting rid of jealousy… getting rid of identity. And there were some who felt that sacrifice worth it.

If it weren't for the heroic actions of a few Global Occult Coalition, humanity as we know it would cease to exist. We still strive to end war and hunger… it is the goal of the United Nations, after all, to promote Peace on Earth. But we have to do it the long hard way. item.content:encoded:
This is one of my favorite articles on this site. I love the little nugget of wholesomeness and implied good ending, which is pretty rare here. I love the flow and the buildup of the story too, though it did seem that Dr. Mary Nakayama escalated pretty quickly from "I want a vacation" to "I want to be God".

As for whether or not this article "makes sense" as a real -001, based on the passivity of the O5 council, I like to think one of them has a prior relationship to Dr. Nakayama, and has reason to trust her, or maybe she's already contacted the O5s, and the line in the containment procedures about directing her to speak with them is just a smokescreen.

Either way, every time I see a researcher catch a break, or an MTF member get lucky, or even when a D-Class narrowly avoids getting eaten by a Big Bad, I wonder if Dr. Nakayama was wathcing out for them. And one line, "Her family will receive a note indicating her love for them." sends chills down my spine every time I read it.

Great job McTiriss! Definite +1.

Here's my two cents.

I didn't really like it. To me it seems that the entire article is leading up to the doctor using SCP-001 to become a god. But the article doesn't really do a good job of establishing the doctor's character. As far as I saw, she found the anomaly, used it for some self-centered purposes, and then decides to become a god. To me, that was an "eye-roll" moment, and I basically thought "really? this person gets to become a god?". The tacked-on romantic disaster thing in the final note just seemed as some sort of whiny (for lack of a better word) rationalization, and didn't make me like the doctor any better.

Perhaps the doctor's "apotheosis" could have been stronger if we saw them use the slot to try and solve some sort of problem, like trying to eliminate a keter-class entity or solving some sort of global health crisis. This would have established the doctor as a good person, and would have made the doctor a character that we could've rooted for. Instead the doctor someone who uses it to get some money, go on vacation, and then decides to become a God. This ending leaves me more annoyed than anything else.

It is possible that the effects of SCP-001 are simply not universal. you will note that all of the alterations she made only affected her site, and possibly The Foundations database, (which can be altered from the database itself from which 001's anomalous properties manifest).

It is completely possible that it is merely a local effect, and that when she requested omnipotence fulfilled it as well as it could, but it was simply not powerful enough to claim dominion over everything.

Alternatively: she explicitly requests to become the godhead, the godhead being the divine nature and power that defines God. (It is the 'what' of god, rather than the 'who', this is important as it changes her nature of existence but not her personality). it is possible that the one true god of the SCP universe exists as the kabbalistic conception of Ein Sof, the limitless nature of god before creation, the one from whom the being we know as 'god' is merely a representation.

God as Ein Sof does not have any attributes, for he is everything. he is the source from which the light of the universe is emanated, and completely beyond human understanding in any meaning of the word. he does not have 'thoughts' or 'actions', for such things would necessarily imply limitations. it is possible that Mary became the godhead, and achieved true omnipotence, only to find that unlimited power is quite a bit more limiting than one might think. and that while she could remake the world, doing so would first require it's destruction. Ein Sof is so much bigger than anything, bigger than everything that merely interacting with the world is enough to bring about it's destruction. So for now Mary sits, outside of time, waiting and watching and hoping that things will become better, knowing that they will become worse. waiting for the point where all hope is lost and there is nothing worth saving, so that she may step in and rewrite the universe, recreating it from the ground up in her own image, a world without monster or demons, a world where the foundation was never needed. our world.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I really liked this one, and it stands out in comparison to a lot of other 001 proposals. I really enjoyed the sort of "by chance" nature of how Nakayama came to become…whatever she is now. I generally like articles which sort of show the "humanity" underneath Foundation procedures, but this one did it especially well by showing the process of how an SCP is created, in universe; a set of (I'm assuming) revisions to the entry, which are continuously revised until they "go live" with the approval of a site director/some other authority. I liked that little glimpse into the world that the april fool's day joke gives: it shows several things, such as that these big time scientists also have time to make jokes when they are just working on entries; and more than that, that between working on these entries, they go to lunch and joke around with each other, much like normal coworkers.

I also like the general idea of the SCP-001 slot changing reality; I've always liked the idea that some aspects of the Foundation, including the database itself, have some level of anomalous properties that even the heads of the Foundation may not be immediately aware of. This article represent the most direct way for the 05s to become aware of their database's anomalous properties, of course, but i like how direct it is.

The only thing I think that bogs this one down is the lengthy letter explaining why she did it. I appreciate the characterization; whereas I know some people on the site don't like characterization, I tend to think it actually gives us a good frame of reference into the Foundation universe so that we can better understand these anomalies. Its easy to get a sense that something is powerful from a description in which SCP-XXXX can kill [REDACTED] number of people in an hour, but these more personal additions to an article help us get a good sense of how individuals, like you or me, would deal with a world that has so much uncertainty. Still, I think the letter gives us a little too much characterization (and characterization that doesn't really serve the "plot" of this entry). It was the one part of the article I was entirely interested in, but I don't think it should necessarily be removed; whereas I was just kinda neutral about it, other people seem to have enjoyed, so I'd leave it in.

Again, great job, and a great 001 proposal that stands out from the rest.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
For one, the O5s don't read every article every day to verify no one made a joke in one of them.

They don't have to.

You see, the whole series is often defined as a database. Sometimes anomalous, sometimes not, but still a database. If the Foundation's IT department is worth its salt, they would have set up triggers that work on database entry updates, determine if the update was significant (as opposed to adding one missing comma), and notify those whom it may concern. It's up to those people to look at the change and investigate it if necessary. Okay, maybe it's not a relational database, maybe it's a system like Sharepoint - still, notifications are a must-have feature in this case.

So it seems that either the IT department is incompetent, or the O5 Council is, or both. Security department sure is - doing nothing while this is developing in front of their eyes.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I know this one's a bit old now, but a few things are being assumed here, and this comment wouldn't fit as nicely elsewhere.

For one, the O5s don't read every article every day to verify no one made a joke in one of them. Really, unless someone is curious about an object they have security rights to know about, or is reviewing an entry to make sure they don't eff something up when going into the containment room, the documents are probably very rarely referenced/looked at by anyone after initial containment, at least for Safe scips that meet the definition of the object class perfectly and can literally just be locked up and forgotten. So, someone in the space of three days making a joke, figuring out what the scip is doing, and ascending to godhood1 before anyone realized it was happening makes sense, particularly if you make the minor assumption that statements made as fact in the document are accepted as such by anyone affected by it. It doesn't appear that everyone who gave her five dollars was being mind controlled. Putting five bucks on her desk was part of how the world was at that point in time after the entry was edited.

The other big assumption is that this is the true SCP-001. How do you know that researcher never existed, and this is another fake story for GOIs to stumble upon? Now they're trying to hack a single .txt file on the Foundation's databases because they think it's the key to "winning" or whatever, instead of attacking every facility everywhere.

Or the researcher existed, but got tired/sick/whatever of working there, so she pretended to disappear in this fantastical way, knowing how the higher ups would respond: No further testing. The things written appear to line up with the facts. Do not investigate. Lock the file. OR the Foundation, after administering an amnestic to her (needed to have her leave the Foundation, but didn't want to terminate her for some reason), came up with the malarkey for the reasons listed in the previous paragraph.

Tl;dr: you assume everything you're being told in the article is the truth. Maybe it is, as far as the writer is concerned, but there is no canon, and coming up with headcanons for things is a good chunk of the fun on this site, at least for me.

Footnotes
1. Why's everyone keep saying godhead, btw? That has a totally different meaning which I don't think is intended. She, as far as anyone knows, became a god, not part of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost godhead that the term would normally be used in reference to.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Technically very well put together. No quibbles with the editing. I'm a fan of the format and style. Plenty to bite into without being overwrought like some of the other entries are.

I find the content to be spectacularly weak though. As a story about the organization, it feels very, very lolfoundation, but not even in a particularly humorous or interesting way. Every aspect and member of the Foundation referenced comes across as at least a little incompetent… except Mary.

As a story about omnipotent godheads it's definitely the dullest one I've ever read. The SCP itself is boring and Mary's ascension feels rushed and the ambiguity at the end of it all feels less like leaving the conclusions up to the reader and more like the story just fails to go anywhere. I also agree with earlier sentiments that it cheapens the rest of the universe it exists in with how trivial and arbitrary it is.

As a story about the character herself, nothing makes me really care about her. She does a few silly things which seem to have no real repercussions at all and then decides to become a god. I appreciate that it's hard to weave a character's backstory into an article, but the final letter feels very forced. I read it and feel less enlightened about her motives and more rolling my eyes at what reads like a hasty attempt to self justify the character at the last minute.

The name "Mary" ends up being very apropos, but for all the wrong reasons. Shame, I like pretty much all of your other stuff, but this is by far the worst.

-1

Apologies for the slight necro-posting, but my personal interpretation is that whoever meddled with the LP actually intended to manipulate the music charts in general to help the album reach #1 (or to keep it there, for whatever reason). However, they screwed up the spell or ritual or virgin sacrifice or whatever they used to make it anomalous in such a way that it ended up only affecting how the album was referenced in digital information, not how it placed in the actual music charts.

ETA: Or, alternatively, that the MacGuffin they used didn't have the effects they thought it would; they didn't realise that the promise on the side of the tin that it would help their album "go straight to #1" was actually referring to a form of data storage that wouldn't be widely used for another fifty years or so.
